## Brief {#brief}

**Research question:** Do drivers rate an infotainment system with voice control as more usable than with touch control?

After a test drive, 160 people filled in an online questionnaire, randomly assigned to one of the two interfaces. You analyse the study once from start to finish, with the tools of the beginner lessons. The only new part is that everything is connected: every number in the report comes from one continuous chain starting at the raw file.

**Analysis plan** (set before the analysis):

| Step | Decision |
|---|---|
| 1 Import | `data/survey.csv`, `interface` as a factor (touch = reference) |
| 2 Exclusion | only respondents who did not answer the attention check with 4; missing single items are no reason |
| 3 Scales | SUS (0–100); trust (1–7, `trust_3`/`trust_5` reversed, ≥ 5 of 6 items); raw TLX (0–100) |
| 4 Main question | SUS between the groups, Welch's t-test, Cohen's d with 95% CI |
| 5 Secondary outcomes | trust and TLX, analysed the same way, reported as secondary outcomes |
| 6 Report | Table 1 by group, results paragraph in APA style |

**How you work:** Each step has one required exercise. It always starts with the correct result of the previous step, so a mistake in step 2 does not carry over. At the end, the [full script](#script) runs all steps in one piece.

## Full script {#script}

The whole analysis in one block, from the file to the text. Change a rule (e.g. `min_valid = 6` or no exclusion) and run the block again: all numbers change with it.

```{webr}
# 1 Import
survey_raw <- read_csv("data/survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(interface = factor(interface, levels = c("touch", "voice")))

# 2 Exclusions (attention check)
cleaned <- survey_raw |>
  filter(attention_check == 4)

# 3 Scale scores
scored <- cleaned |>
  mutate(
    across(c(sus_01, sus_03, sus_05, sus_07, sus_09), \(x) x - 1),
    across(c(sus_02, sus_04, sus_06, sus_08, sus_10), \(x) 5 - x),
    across(c(trust_3, trust_5), \(x) 8 - x),
    sus = 25 * rowMeans(pick(sus_01:sus_10), na.rm = TRUE),
    trust = row_means(pick(trust_1:trust_6), min_valid = 5),
    tlx = rowMeans(pick(starts_with("tlx_")), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(respondent, interface, age, gender, tech_affinity, sus, trust, tlx)

# 4 Main question and effect sizes
sus_test <- t.test(sus ~ interface, data = scored)
cohens_d(sus ~ interface, data = scored)
cohens_d(trust ~ interface, data = scored)
cohens_d(tlx ~ interface, data = scored)

# 5 Report: sample, result text, Table 1
c(raw = nrow(survey_raw), excluded = nrow(survey_raw) - nrow(cleaned), analysed = nrow(scored))
report(sus_test, data = scored)
tbl_summary(
  scored,
  by = interface,
  include = c(age, gender, tech_affinity, sus, trust, tlx),
  type = tech_affinity ~ "continuous",
  statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
  label = list(
    age ~ "Age (years)", gender ~ "Gender", tech_affinity ~ "Affinity for technology (1–5)",
    sus ~ "SUS (0–100)", trust ~ "Trust (1–7)", tlx ~ "NASA-TLX raw (0–100)"
  )
)
```

**How to report it:**

> *Method.* Of 160 respondents, three were excluded for failing the attention check; 157 were analysed (79 touch, 78 voice). Trust was computed when at least five of six items were answered (four respondents without a score). Table 1 describes the sample by group.
>
> *Results.* Voice control was rated as more usable than touch control (SUS *M* = 61.5 vs. 51.1; difference 10.4 points, 95% CI [2.7, 18.0], *t*(154.85) = 2.67, *p* = .008, *d* = 0.43, 95% CI [0.11, 0.74]). Both means are below the benchmark of 68. For the secondary outcomes, the differences were small and uncertain (trust: *d* = 0.14 [−0.18, 0.45]; workload: *d* = −0.21 [−0.53, 0.10], each voice − touch).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Run locally

In the browser, the report stays on the page. Locally, you write it as a Quarto document; text, numbers and table then come straight from R and change with the data:

````markdown
---
title: "Voice vs. touch control"
format: docx
---

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(datawizard)
library(effectsize)
library(gtsummary)
# ... steps 1–3 from the full script ...
sus_test <- t.test(sus ~ interface, data = scored)
sus_d <- cohens_d(sus ~ voice_first, data = mutate(scored, voice_first = fct_rev(interface)))
```

Voice was rated `r round(diff(sus_test$estimate), 1)` SUS points higher,
d = `r round(sus_d$Cohens_d, 2)`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sample
tbl_summary(scored, by = interface, include = c(age, gender, tech_affinity))
```
````

Result: a Word file that is automatically correct the next time you render it with new data or changed rules. `fct_rev()` reverses the levels so that d is positive for an advantage of voice.
:::

## Checklist {#cheatsheet}

```r
# One object per step, each from the previous one
survey_raw <- read_csv("data/survey.csv") |> mutate(interface = factor(...))
cleaned    <- survey_raw |> filter(attention_check == 4)
scored     <- cleaned |> mutate(<reverse>, <scale scores>) |> select(...)

t.test(sus ~ interface, data = scored)        # main question
cohens_d(sus ~ interface, data = scored)      # effect size + CI
tbl_summary(scored, by = interface, ...)      # Table 1
report(t.test(...), data = scored)            # draft text, then check it
```

- Analysis plan before the analysis: exclusions, scoring rules, main and secondary outcomes.
- After importing, `glimpse()`: types, factor levels, number of rows.
- Report exclusions with number and reason; Table 1 and test on the same sample.
- Check the sign (first factor level minus second), state the direction in words.
- Non-significant does not mean "no difference": look at the CI.
- Everything in one script or Quarto document, no retyped numbers.
